sections.h2: What is the Florida homestead exemption worth to an owner?
sections.html:
It shields as much as $50,000 of assessed value from tax, delivered in two layers. Per the state's homestead guide (pt113), the first $25,000 offsets every levy, school taxes included. A further $25,000 applies only to assessed value past the $50,000 mark and skips school taxes.

That second layer moves with inflation. When the CPI change is positive, the amount is adjusted on each January 1; when negative, it holds steady. The department's table starts from a 2024 base, so look at your own bill or ask the appraiser for the amount in force.

The exemption lowers the taxable base and nothing more. Whatever millage the school board, county, city and special districts set still applies to the remainder.

sections.h2: Who qualifies, and what ends the exemption?
sections.html:
Title in your name on January 1, plus permanent residence status by that same day, is the entry ticket. You get one permanent residence at a time.

Three events end it, according to the guide:

  • You rent the unit out.
  • The house stops being your permanent home.
  • You stop being a Florida permanent resident.

Servicemembers have an exception in s. 196.061, which lets them lease the home without abandoning homestead (pt109). Everyone else who relocates should tell the appraiser so a stale exemption does not linger on the roll.

sections.h2: How do I apply, and what if the claim is denied?
sections.html:
Form DR-501 goes to your county appraiser, and the state calendar treats the first of March as the cutoff for exemptions and agricultural classifications (taxpayer calendar).

A denial letter starts a 30 day countdown for a value adjustment board petition. Disputing the value is a separate route: a DR-486 petition filed with the clerk of court within 25 days of the Notice of Proposed Property Taxes, which arrives in August.

Appraisers decide who is eligible and tax collectors mail the bills. When you are unsure which office owns a problem, begin with the appraiser.

sections.h2: What does Save Our Homes do for a long-time owner?
sections.html:
It throttles annual growth in a homestead's assessed value. After the first year, an increase cannot beat the smaller of 3 percent and the CPI change, and assessed value can never pass just value (pt112).

The department's chart, revised in January 2026, lists:

YearCPI changeCap applied
20243.4%3.0%
20252.9%2.9%
20262.7%2.7%

Source: Save Our Homes cap chart. The 2024 row shows the 3 percent ceiling biting while inflation ran higher.

Property without homestead faces a ceiling of 10 percent per year, from the same calendar page.

sections.h2: What happens to the cap when a homestead sells?
sections.html:
The accumulated protection disappears. A sale, foreclosure or any transfer of legal or beneficial title counts as a change of ownership, and the next January 1 the parcel returns to just value. Listed exceptions include spousal transfers and certain transfers at death.

Your exemption stays behind as well. A buyer who moves in applies fresh, and a buyer who rents the place out cannot claim it. The gap between your old bill and the new owner's first full bill can be large for a house held many years.

The tax year of a closing in the spring or summer still carries the assessment fixed the previous January, and the November bill is split under the purchase contract. Read that clause before you sign.

sections.h2: Can I carry my Save Our Homes savings to another house?
sections.html:
Portability allows it when you meet the timing rule. The new homestead must be established within three years counted from January 1 of the year you gave up the old one, not from the closing date. Form DR-501T travels with the DR-501 (pt112).

Statute text lowers the new assessed value by the lesser of $500,000 or the old home's difference between just and assessed value (s. 193.155(8)). The statute page records that ch. 2026-239 amendments first reach the 2027 roll, so ask the appraiser which version governs your move (s. 193.155).

sections.h2: Are there added breaks for seniors, veterans and disabled owners?
sections.html:
Several, layered on the base exemption, and local governments control some of them.

  • 65 and older: an ordinance may add up to $50,000 where household income stays within the limit, which began at $20,000 and is indexed by CPI (s. 196.075(2)).
  • 65 and older, 25 years a permanent resident, just value below $250,000: an ordinance may exempt the whole assessed value, income limit permitting.
  • Veterans 65 and older with a permanent service-connected disability: a discount equal to the VA disability percentage, which passes to an unremarried surviving spouse (s. 196.082).
  • Disabled former servicemembers rated 10 percent or more: $5,000 off assessed value (ss. 196.081, 196.091).
  • Total and permanent service-connected disability: a possible full exemption on the homestead.

Details are in the state's guides for seniors and veterans. Ask your appraiser which of these your county adopted.

Part of it can. Form DR-570 reaches the tax collector by March 31 after the assessment year. Deferral covers tax beyond 5 percent of the previous year's household income, or everything when income is under $10,000. Permanent residents 65 and older may defer the slice beyond 3 percent of income.

On payment, the November bill carries a 4 percent discount, December 3, January 2 and February 1. Unpaid amounts go delinquent on April 1 and certificates are sold by June 1 (calendar). A deferral recorded on your home can be cleared with a payoff figure from the tax collector, so request one before listing.

sections.h2: What should a seller with a homestead check before listing?
sections.html:
Open the appraiser's parcel record first. It lists assessed value, just value and exemption status. The distance between those two values is what Save Our Homes has kept off your bill.

  • Confirm the current exemption application was accepted.
  • Note any senior, veteran or disability benefit, since none transfers to a buyer.
  • Find out whether a DR-570 deferral is on record.
  • Decide early whether you intend to port the benefit, because that starts a three year window.

Share the answers with the closing agent so the buyer's own filing can be planned.

It also pays to pull the last two tax bills. Compare the line for each taxing body, because school, county and city rates differ, and a buyer's agent will likely do the same exercise. Seeing which levies the exemption actually reduces tells you whether the buyer's real cost after reassessment is close to yours or far above it. If you recently remodeled, ask the appraiser whether new improvements were added to the roll, since additions can raise just value on their own.

faqs.q: When must a Florida homestead claim be filed?
faqs.a: The first of March, with the county appraiser, using Form DR-501, and you must have made the home your permanent residence by January 1. A denial goes to the value adjustment board, and that petition has a 30 day window running from the mailing of the denial letter.

faqs.q: How big is the Florida homestead exemption?
faqs.a: Up to $50,000 in assessed value. The initial $25,000 offsets all taxes, school levies included. The extra $25,000 touches only value above $50,000 and excludes school taxes. That extra amount is indexed to inflation.

faqs.q: Does a buyer inherit my Save Our Homes cap?
faqs.a: No. Sale means a change of ownership and a return to just value the following January 1. Spouse transfers and certain transfers at death are among the exceptions.

faqs.q: Can I keep my cap savings when I buy elsewhere in Florida?
faqs.a: Often, through portability. Establish the new homestead within three years counted from January 1 of the year you abandoned the old one, and file DR-501T with DR-501. The reduction cannot exceed $500,000 or the old home's just-minus-assessed gap, whichever is lower.

faqs.q: What if I rent my homestead out?
faqs.a: Renting costs you the exemption, as does moving away or leaving Florida as a permanent resident. Servicemembers are the listed exception under s. 196.061.
